newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right puts Europe on the election line.
newsitem.headline: French right puts Europe on the election line.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe issued fresh warnings on Wednesday that a left-wing victory in forthcoming parliamentary elections would set off a European crisis and jeopardise the single European currency.

Four days from the poll's first round, he said the Socialist Party's conditions to join the euro could not be met and repeated President Jacques Chirac's warning that power-sharing with a left-wing government would prevent France speaking with a single voice on Europe.
"The conditions set by (Socialist leader Lionel) Mr Jospin for the euro are geared to make it fail," he said.

Juppe seized on a Communist Party statement that it would consider it a breach of its election pact with the Socialists if a left-wing government stuck to the Maastricht timetable for joining the euro in 1999.
"If this side won a majority, it would no longer be a cacophony but a genuine divorce," he told France 2 television.
Francis Wurtz, who heads the Communist Party's international department, said France could not meet Maastricht criteria without a new round of austerity, something the left has pledged not to impose.
Jospin retorted that both conservatives and Communists were drawing closer to the conditions he set for joining the euro -- a more flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty criteria.
Juppe said a sense of history would override a narrow view of "the nth decimal" in making European monetary union.

In an interview to be published on Thursday in the business daily Les Echos, Juppe announced plans for a fresh batch of privatisations, possibly including national airline Air France and bank Credit Lyonnais this year, to be followed by insurance group Gan and its banking arm CIC.
The sale of aircraft-maker Aerospatiale-Dassault and defence electronics group Thomson-CSF is already under way.
Jospin said more privatisation was an admission of failure by the government. "They need to privatise companies only to balance their budget," he told TF1 television.

While the opposition insisted on the government's failure to curb record 12.8 percent unemployment, Chirac delivered an upbeat assessment of the economy, trumpeting two big export contracts signed just in time for the election --- a major sale of Airbus planes to China and a warship deal with Saudi Arabia.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Chirac told the last cabinet meeting before polling day that the "spirit of enterprise and the spirit of conquest were back".
Jospin said the campaign against "cohabitation", the French term for power-sharing between a president and government of opposing parties, showed the right was running scared.
"It carries no weight (because) no one can put the French people under duress. In this election, the French people will express themselves freely," he told a news conference.
Justice Minister Jacques Toubon acknowledged concern in the ruling coalition at the prospect of a very close outcome.
"The election is tight," he told Europe 1 radio. "We would be most imprudent to be boastful or complacent."

French financial markets were stable on Wednesday, with the franc steady against the German mark and the Paris bourse up 1.1 percent buoyed by Wall Street's rally after the Federal Reserve Board decided against raising interest rates.

Opinion polls released last weekend before a legal ban on publication of such surveys showed the centre-right in the lead but the combined forces of Socialists, Communists and ecologists gaining ground and within striking distance of a victory.
No more polls may be published before the June 1 conclusion of the two-round election, although surveys continue to be taken and some may be visible on the Internet.
